description:
We are a technology-driven team, InfoVerse Cosmos, passionate about AI, space technology, Earth observation and solving real-world challenges.

For this challenge, we aim to combine Dancing with the SARs NASA satellite data, AI/ML, geospatial analytics and GeoSAR Intelligence insights to develop an intelligent decision-support platform for Earthian.

We welcome developers, data scientists, GIS experts,  researchers and creative problem-solvers who want to build impactful technology.
summary:
Every monsoon, the people who manage our floodplains face the same problem: when the water matters most, they cannot see it. Clouds sit over the rivers for weeks, so ordinary satellite photos go dark, and the flood maps that do exist only show open water — they miss the water hiding under tall grass, paddy, and trees, which is exactly where wetlands, wildlife, and village fields live.

We built GeoSAR Drishti to give that view back. It uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L‑band radar, which sees straight through cloud and reaches partly under the canopy, across a whole monsoon season. From that radar it shows three things a flood photo never could: where water is open versus hidden under plants, how many satellite passes each place stayed wet (we call it “M of N observations,” never “days flooded”), and which roads and villages were wet again and again — so a field team knows where to look first.
details:
Detailed Project Description — What it does, how it works, and what we hope to achieve

What it does. GeoSAR Drishti is an interactive web console that turns a season of NISAR radar passes into a clear water story. You pick an area, scrub through the monsoon on a time slider, and switch between two simple map layers — open water and water hidden under plants — or a repeatedly-wet layer that darkens the more often a place was wet. Click anywhere and it reads the full radar history of that exact spot and explains, in plain language, what the satellite saw. A one-click report summarises the whole area, and an “inspection log” ranks the roads and settlements that kept intersecting wet pixels.

How it works. A NISAR L‑band pulse reflects very differently off the three surfaces we care about: calm open water acts like a mirror and looks dark; water trapped under vegetation bounces the signal back brighter (a “double-bounce”); dry land sits in between. Our pipeline reads only the slice of each (multi-gigabyte) radar file that covers the area, filters speckle, converts to decibels, and classifies every pixel on every date — open water by a per-scene brightness threshold, hidden water by a +3 dB brightness jump against a dry reference. We then count, per pixel, how many passes it was wet (the hydroperiod), cluster the ever-wet areas into named water regimes with an unsupervised model, and intersect the result with OpenStreetMap roads and villages to list places worth inspecting first. The pipeline can also cross-check open water against JRC historical water and OPERA DSWx when those files are supplied; they are not loaded in the demo areas.

Two audiences, one console. A top-bar toggle switches between a Simple view (plain words, satellite backdrop, no jargon — for a curious citizen or a district officer) and a Scientist view (decibel trajectories, per-scene thresholds, granule/track provenance). We wanted a schoolchild and a hydrologist to both feel at home on the same screen.

Built to never break in front of a judge. The backend wraps every response in a predictable envelope and falls back gracefully if the network, NASA servers, or an optional AI are slow — the demo keeps working offline, and the app clearly labels whether it is live, cached, or offline.

What we hope to achieve. We want wetland managers, protected-area wardens, and district disaster planners to start the monsoon with a map of where water actually goes, how long it lingers, and which roads and settlements deserve an early ground check — turning a cloudy, invisible season into something they can plan around.

Tools & tech. Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Tailwind, Recharts, Zustand. Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, h5py, scikit-learn, geopandas, osmnx. All the water science is deterministic math we wrote and checked ourselves.
